controls.title: Sightlines from occupied spaces
controls.objective: Entrances, parking, and approaches are visible from regularly occupied interior spaces.

evidence.description: Photo from inside showing the view, or its obstruction

questions.text: Can the main entrance, parking, and building approaches be seen from regularly occupied rooms (reception, offices) through clear glazing?
questions.guidance: Stand at reception and occupied offices. Partial: views blocked by film, blinds kept closed, or storage. Photograph obstructions.

controls.title: Landscaping for visibility
controls.objective: Shrubs and tree canopies near paths, entrances, and windows do not block views or provide concealment.

evidence.description: Photo of each overgrown area with a height reference

questions.text: Within 10 ft (3 m) of paths, entrances, and windows, are shrubs kept at 3 ft (0.9 m) or lower and tree canopies raised to 7 ft (2.1 m) or higher?
questions.guidance: Measure representative plantings. Many CPTED guides use a 2 to 3 ft shrub and 6 to 8 ft canopy rule; local codes vary (unverified). Photograph overgrowth.

references.source: Crowe and Fennelly, Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, 3rd ed., 2013

controls.title: Defined territory
controls.objective: Transitions from public to semi-private to private space are marked by visible physical cues.

evidence.description: Photo of each boundary between public and private space

questions.text: Is the change from public to private space marked by a visible feature (signage, paving change, low fence, gate, or landscaping) at every approach?
questions.guidance: Walk each approach from the street. Partial: some approaches unmarked.

controls.title: Wayfinding to a single public entrance
controls.objective: Visitors are guided to a designated public entrance and other entrances are marked for staff only.

questions.text: Do signs and path layout lead visitors from parking to one designated public entrance, with other doors marked staff only or emergency exit only?
questions.guidance: Follow the route a first-time visitor would take. Partial: signage present but paths lead to staff doors.

controls.title: Maintenance and image
controls.objective: Graffiti, litter, broken fixtures, and abandoned items are removed or repaired within a defined time.

questions.text: Number of graffiti marks, broken fixtures, litter accumulations, or abandoned items observed during the exterior walk
questions.guidance: Count distinct items on the exterior walk.

questions.text: Is there a written maximum time to remove graffiti and repair vandalism (for example 48 hours), and was it met for the last 3 incidents?
questions.guidance: Partial: target defined but not met.

references.source: Crowe and Fennelly, Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, 3rd ed., 2013

controls.title: Activity support in common areas
controls.objective: Outdoor common areas have features or programs that draw legitimate use during operating hours.

evidence.description: Observation of common area use during the visit

questions.text: Do outdoor common areas have seating, amenities, or scheduled activities that bring legitimate users during operating hours?
questions.guidance: Partial: features present but area observed unused and isolated.

references.source: Crowe and Fennelly, Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, 3rd ed., 2013

controls.title: Concealment and entrapment areas
controls.objective: Recessed doorways, alcoves, and spaces behind structures along routes offer no hiding spots, or are lit and covered by surveillance.

questions.text: Number of concealment or entrapment spots along pedestrian routes that are neither lit, mirrored, nor covered by a camera
questions.guidance: A spot is any space where a person can stand unseen from the route within 6 ft (1.8 m) of it.

references.source: Crowe and Fennelly, Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, 3rd ed., 2013
